name: Spectral evidence
statement: Testimony that the accused person's spectre had tormented a witness, admitted at Salem in 1692, where only the witness could see the spectre.
meaning: The claim on trial was that a witch sent her shape, or spectre, to afflict a victim while her body stood elsewhere. The evidence for it was the afflicted person's account of what she saw. Nobody else in the courtroom could see the spectre, so nothing the accused said or did could weigh against the testimony, and her presence in the dock was consistent with it. Whether that testimony could convict turned on one question of theology. John Hale, minister at Beverly and a witness to the proceedings, listed the principles the court worked from. He put this one first: that the Devil could not assume the shape of an innocent person in doing mischief unto mankind, for if the Lord should suffer him in this he would subvert the course of humane Justice, by bringing men to suffer for what he did in their Shapes. Grant that principle and the spectre identifies the witch, because the Devil can only wear a guilty face. Deny it and the same testimony proves nothing about the person whose face was worn. Increase Mather denied it. His Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits Personating Men opens on exactly that question: whether Satan may appear in the Shape of an Innocent and Pious, as well as of a Nocent and Wicked Person. The answer is that the Devil may by Divine Permission appear in the shape of Innocent and Pious Persons.

origin.who: The Court of Oyer and Terminer, Salem
origin.note: The commission creating the court was issued on 27 May 1692, and instructed it to hear and determine all manner of crimes according to the law and custom of England and of the province. The phrase is the participants' own. Governor Sir William Phips, writing to London on 12 October 1692, described prisoners with only spectre evidence against them, and Robert Calef used spectre evidence for what the January 1693 juries asked the bench about. The doctrine is older than the outbreak: the principle Hale places first was, by Burr's note, the answer the Connecticut ministers gave their court in 1669 in almost the same words.

evidence: The court's record is the evidence, and it runs one way until the rule changes. Calef's session by session account has Bridget Bishop condemned first and executed on 10 June. Five were tried on 30 June and these were all condemned that Sessions. Six were tried on 5 August and these were all brought in Guilty and Condemned. Six more were tried on 9 September and nine on 17 September, all sentenced to death. Nineteen were hanged. Giles Corey was pressed to death on 16 September for refusing to plead, which Linder describes as a man of over eighty pressed under heavy stones for refusing to submit to trial. What happened when a jury did acquit is on the record too. The jury returned not guilty for Rebecca Nurse and the accusers in court cried out. One judge said he was not satisfied, the chief judge pointed the jury back to a remark of hers, and the jury went out again and convicted. The foreman Thomas Fisk set his reasons down in writing on 4 July 1692. Phips ended that court on 29 October. The General Court created a Superior Court of Judicature on 25 November and, by a supplementary act of 16 December, sent it to Essex on 3 January 1693. Calef reports the result at Salem: ignoramus was returned on the bills against thirty, billa vera against twenty six more, and of all these three only were found Guilty by the Jewry upon Trial. When the jurors asked the bench what account they ought to make of the spectre evidence, the answer was as much as of Chips in Wort. At Charlestown at the end of January, Calef writes, the Spectre-Evidence was not made use of in these Tryals, so that the Jewry soon brought her in not Guilty, and the rest tried with Sarah Daston were acquitted as well. Phips gave London his own count on 21 February 1692/3: all that were brought to tryall to the number of fifety two, were cleared saving three. He reprieved those three and five condemned by the earlier court, on the Attorney General's advice that there was the same reason to clear the three condemned as the rest. Stoughton left the bench and came no more that Court.

replication.headline: No replication record exists for a seventeenth-century rule of evidence, and none was found. What the page rests on is the court record, which is a single documented case rather than a repeated measurement.
replication.detail: Searches of Crossref by bibliographic query, CourtListener's opinion database, the Caselaw Access Project, Open Library and general web search located no experimental or statistical study that tests spectral evidence as a claim about judgement. Crossref returns historical scholarship, including Craker's article in The Historical Journal and Owen's essay on the witchcraft cosmology of Salem Village, and nothing that repeats an observation. The nearest thing to a rate on this page is a contrast within one episode rather than a replication. Two courts drawn largely from the same bench sat months apart on overlapping charges, with spectral testimony ruled worthless in between. Every session of the first ended in condemnation, and the second, by Calef's count, returned three convictions on twenty six true bills. That is one before and after in one jurisdiction, and no second jurisdiction was located that changed the rule and recorded what followed.

limits: Craker's article is the most direct scholarly treatment located and it could not be read. Cambridge's own PDF link returns a holding page, and everything attributed to it here comes from the abstract in its Crossref record. Hoffer's legal history and Rosenthal's edition of the records were not obtained; Hoffer is named because the Massachusetts Appeals Court cites him for its definition, not because this entry read him. The counts do not reconcile. Calef's thirty ignoramus bills and twenty six true bills make fifty six, and Phips reports fifty two brought to trial, and no source located resolves the two. Calef was a hostile witness writing in 1697 with an argument to make, and Phips was writing to London about his own conduct with his enemies in mind, so both counts are interested. Cases of Conscience was read in the Internet Archive's uncorrected OCR of the 1693 Boston printing, which is legible in places and broken in others; the passages quoted here were checked against David Levin's quotations of the same pages. No conviction rate for the Court of Oyer and Terminer is quoted, because no source located states one, and the session tallies above are what Calef prints rather than a total computed from them. Searches covered Crossref, CourtListener, the Caselaw Access Project, the Internet Archive, Open Library and general web search. Cambridge Core, Justia, Casetext and the Michigan text of the Evans edition all refused requests, so absence of a document here means absence from the places that answered.
misreadings: The story that Increase Mather stopped the trials compresses two things that did not happen together. Levin read the book against the ministers' advice of 15 June 1692. He shows that Cases of Conscience leaves two grounds standing on which a witch may still be justly convicted: a free and voluntary confession, and the sworn testimony of two credible persons to acts none but a familiar of the Devil could perform. Immediately after endorsing that second ground Mather writes that it were better that Ten Suspected Witches should escape, than that one Innocent Person should be Condemned, and the two sentences sit on the same page. In the postscript he says that of George Burroughs, the one trial he attended, he could not have acquitted him. The book was read to the ministers on 3 October 1692, after the last eight hangings on 22 September, and Levin's judgement is that the attack on spectral evidence helped prevent further executions rather than that Mather alone ended them. The supposed split between father and son is the second error. Both Mathers denied it, Increase wrote that he perused and approved his son's book before it was printed, and Cotton said the same privately to his uncle on 20 October 1692. Levin argues the two books were complementary. Third, spectral testimony was not the whole of what the earlier court heard. Craker's abstract states that no one charged only with spectral appearance was even tried, and that the non-spectral acts were what drew the court's attention, which he calls the reverse of the standard claim. Rebecca Nurse's conviction turned on a remark she made in the room. Fourth, the name is shared. Spectral Evidence, the 1997 book by Moira Johnston, is a Houghton Mifflin account of the Ramona case on recovered memory in Napa Valley, and is not about Salem. Open Library lists the same title on a 2002 MIT Press book by Ulrich Baer, a 2018 novel by Gemma Files and a 2023 Litmus Press book by Elizabeth Willis and Nancy Bowen. Where the term does travel is by analogy. Douglas J., dissenting in State v. Dustin in 1982, called a prosecutor's appeal to what went through a witness's mind reminiscent of the spectral evidence admitted in the seventeenth century Salem witch trials. The Massachusetts Appeals Court in Commonwealth v. Coutu in 2015 heard counsel liken a victim's energy recognition testimony to it, disagreed, and defined the term as witness testimony that the accused person's spirit or spectral shape appeared to the witness.

sources.text: Mather, I. (1693). Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits Personating Men, Witchcrafts, Infallible Proofs of Guilt in Such as Are Accused with That Crime. Boston: printed and sold by Benjamin Harris at the London Coffee-House. Read in the Internet Archive's uncorrected OCR of the Early English Books scan. Source for the first question, for the answer that the Devil may appear in the shape of innocent and pious persons, for the ten suspected witches passage, and for the fourteen ministers who signed the preface.

Burr, G. L. (Ed.) (1914). Narratives of the Witchcraft Cases, 1648-1706. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. Read in the Internet Archive's full text. Source for Phips's letters of 12 October 1692 and 21 February 1692/3, for Hale's Modest Enquiry including the first great principle and the nineteen executed, for Calef's More Wonders including the trial tallies, the Nurse verdict, the January 1693 court, the chips in wort answer and the jurors' recantation, and for Burr's notes on the dates of the commission and the new court.

Levin, D. (1985). Did the Mathers disagree about the Salem witchcraft trials? Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society, pages 19 to 37. Read in full as a PDF from the Society. Source for the reading of Cases of Conscience, for the two grounds of conviction it leaves standing, for the dates of 15 June and 3 October 1692 and 20 October 1692, and for the argument that the Mathers cooperated.

Craker, W. D. (1997). Spectral evidence, non-spectral acts of witchcraft, and confession at Salem in 1692. The Historical Journal, 40(2), 331-358. The full text could not be obtained; the claim that no one charged only with spectral appearance was tried is quoted from the abstract in the Crossref record.

Linder, D. (2007). The Witchcraft Trials in Salem: A Commentary. SSRN working paper. Described here from its abstract, which is the source for the nineteen hanged between June and September 1692 and for the man of over eighty pressed to death.

State v. Dustin, 122 N.H. 544 (1982). Read from the Caselaw Access Project's JSON of the official reports. Source for the sentence in Douglas J.'s dissent comparing the prosecution's statements to spectral evidence.

Commonwealth v. Coutu, 88 Mass. App. Ct. 686 (2015). Read from the Caselaw Access Project's JSON of the official reports. Source for the court's definition of spectral evidence and its refusal of the analogy to energy recognition testimony; the footnote cites Hoffer, The Salem Witchcraft Trials: A Legal History, at 78-79, and Starkey, The Devil in Massachusetts, at 54 and 93.

Johnston, M. (1997). Spectral Evidence: The Ramona Case: Incest, Memory, and Truth on Trial in Napa Valley. Boston: Houghton Mifflin. ISBN 0395718228. Cited only to identify the book that shares the name; its contents were not read for this entry.

Superior Court of Judicature: Witchcraft Trials, January to May 1693, SWP No. 170, transcribed from the Records of the Superior Court of Judicature (1692/3) held at the Massachusetts State Archives. The trial records themselves; consulted, and no count on this page is derived from tallying them.
